questions.q: State the rotational analogue of Newton's second law for a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis. Write the formula with SI units for each quantity.
questions.a: The rotational analogue is τ = Iα, where τ is net external torque (N·m), I is moment of inertia about the axis (kg·m²), and α is angular acceleration (rad/s²). A wrong answer (e.g., τ = Iω or F = mrα) reveals confusion between torque and force, or between angular acceleration and angular velocity, or mixing linear and rotational quantities.

questions.q: Explain why the moment of inertia (I) plays the same role in rotational motion as mass (m) plays in linear motion. Use the kinetic energy expressions to justify your answer.
questions.a: Linear kinetic energy is K = ½mv²; rotational kinetic energy is K = ½Iω². Since ω is the rotational analogue of v, I must be the analogue of m. Both quantify inertia – resistance to change in motion. A wrong answer (e.g., "I is mass times radius") shows the student memorised a formula but doesn't understand the dynamical role of I as the coefficient linking torque to angular acceleration, just as m links force to linear acceleration.

questions.q: A constant torque of 5.0 N·m is applied to a flywheel with moment of inertia 0.40 kg·m², initially at rest. (a) Find its angular acceleration. (b) Find its angular velocity after 10 s. (c) Calculate the work done by the torque in this time.
questions.a:
(a) α = τ/I = 5.0 / 0.40 = 12.5 rad/s².  
(b) ω = ω₀ + αt = 0 + (12.5)(10) = 125 rad/s.  
(c) θ = ½αt² = ½(12.5)(100) = 625 rad. Work W = τθ = (5.0)(625) = 3125 J.  
Check via work-energy: ½Iω² = ½(0.40)(125)² = 3125 J. Matches.  
A wrong answer in (c) using W = τωt (confusing power with work) or forgetting the ½ in θ reveals misunderstanding of rotational kinematics or work-energy theorem.

questions.q: Two bodies – a hollow cylinder and a solid sphere – have the same mass (2.0 kg) and radius (0.10 m). Identical torques are applied to each about their symmetry axes. Which acquires a greater angular speed after 5.0 s? Justify using moments of inertia.
questions.a:
For hollow cylinder: I_cyl = MR² = (2.0)(0.10)² = 0.020 kg·m².  
For solid sphere: I_sph = ⅖MR² = 0.4 × 0.020 = 0.008 kg·m².  
Same τ ⇒ α = τ/I. Smaller I gives larger α. Sphere has smaller I, so larger α, thus larger ω after same time.  
A wrong answer choosing the cylinder reveals the misconception that "more mass at the rim gives more angular acceleration" – confusing moment of inertia with torque production.

questions.q: A student solves this problem: "A grindstone (solid disk, M = 10 kg, R = 0.20 m) rotates at 300 rpm. A friction force of 20 N is applied tangentially at the rim. Find the time to stop." Their solution: τ = FR = 4 N·m, I = ½MR² = 0.2 kg·m², α = τ/I = 20 rad/s², ω₀ = 300 rpm = 300 rad/s, t = ω₀/α = 15 s. Identify the error(s) and give the correct time.
questions.a:
Error 1: ω₀ = 300 rpm = 300 × 2π/60 = 10π ≈ 31.4 rad/s, not 300 rad/s.  
Error 2: Friction torque opposes motion, so α = -20 rad/s².  
Correct: t = ω₀/|α| = 31.4 / 20 ≈ 1.57 s.  
A wrong answer keeping 300 rad/s shows failure to convert rpm to rad/s – a very common unit-conversion error in rotational dynamics.

questions.q: Design a simple school-lab experiment to verify τ = Iα using a rotating platform (like a lazy Susan), a hanging mass on a string wound around the axle, and a stopwatch. List the measurements needed and how you would compute I experimentally.
questions.a:
Measure: axle radius r, hanging mass m, time t for mass to fall distance h.  
Compute linear acceleration a = 2h/t². Torque τ = (mg - ma)r ≈ mgr if a << g. Angular acceleration α = a/r.  
Then I = τ/α = (mgr) / (a/r) = mgr²/a.  
Plot τ vs α for different m; slope gives I.  
A poor answer that ignores the tension in the string (using τ = mgr exactly) or doesn't convert linear to angular quantities reveals incomplete understanding of the torque-acceleration relationship.
